module_title: Installing PVC Pipes for Outdoor and Agricultural Use

lessons.title: Using PVC for Irrigation Lines in Small Farms
lessons.body:
For small farms in Africa, PVC pipes are a cheap and strong way to move water from a source to your crops. Use uPVC (unplasticized PVC) pipes because they handle pressure and sunlight better than thin garden hoses. The most common sizes are 20mm, 25mm, and 32mm diameter. For a half-acre plot, a 25mm main line works well. You will need a hacksaw or PVC cutter, a tape measure, a marking pencil, PVC primer and cement (glue), and fittings like elbows, tees, and couplings. 

Start by planning your layout. Measure from your water source (tap, tank, or pump) to the farthest point. Dig trenches 30â40 cm deep to bury the main line. This protects pipes from sun and farm tools. Lay pipes in the trench, dry-fit all fittings first. Cut pipes squarely with a hacksaw, then remove burrs with sandpaper. Apply primer to both pipe and fitting, then cement, and twist a quarter turn. Hold for 30 seconds. Let joints cure for at least 2 hours before running water. 

For a typical small farm, use a pump that delivers at least 20 liters per minute at 1 bar pressure. If your water source is a tank, place it at least 2 meters above the field for gravity flow. Install a filter (screen or sand) at the pump outlet to stop debris blocking sprinklers. Use a pressure gauge to check you stay below 4 bar for uPVC. 

Remember to include a drain valve at the lowest point to empty pipes after irrigation. This prevents algae and mosquito breeding. In sandy soil, add a 10 cm layer of sand around pipes to prevent abrasion. In clay soil, backfill carefully to avoid cracking. Test the system by running water and checking for leaks. Fix any leak immediately with a repair coupling. A well-installed PVC irrigation line can last 10â15 years with basic care.

lessons.title: Handling UV Exposure: Painting or Burying Pipes
lessons.body:
PVC pipes break down under strong African sun. Ultraviolet (UV) rays make the plastic brittle, causing cracks and leaks within 2â3 years if left exposed. You must either bury pipes or paint them. Burying is best for main lines. Dig trenches 30â40 cm deep and cover pipes completely. This also protects from animals and farm machinery. If you cannot bury, paint exposed pipes with a light-colored acrylic or latex paint. Light colors reflect heat. Do not use oil-based paint; it can damage PVC. 

Before painting, clean the pipe with a damp cloth to remove dust. Let it dry. Apply two coats of paint, allowing 2 hours between coats. Paint fittings and valves too. Reapply every 2â3 years. In very hot areas, you can also wrap pipes with aluminum foil tape or shade cloth, but painting is cheaper. 

For above-ground lines that must stay exposed, use UV-resistant PVC pipes (often gray or dark gray). These cost about 20% more but last 5â7 years longer. Even then, painting adds extra protection. If you use drip tape or thin-walled pipes, always bury them or cover with mulch. 

In off-season, store unused pipes indoors or under shade. Never leave them in direct sun. When repairing, use UV-resistant cement. Check exposed pipes monthly for chalky white powder (UV damage). If you see it, sand lightly and repaint. Burying is the cheapest long-term solution. For a small farm, bury all main lines and only leave risers and sprinklers above ground. This saves money on paint and replacement.

lessons.title: Installing Valves and Sprinklers for Garden Irrigation
lessons.body:
Valves control water flow to different sections of your garden. Start with a gate valve or ball valve at the main line. Ball valves are better because they open and close with a quarter turn. Install them using PVC primer and cement. For a garden, use 20mm or 25mm valves. Place a valve at the start of each branch line so you can water one area at a time. 

Sprinklers come in many types. For small gardens, use impact sprinklers or micro-sprinklers. Impact sprinklers cover 10â15 meters diameter and need 1.5â2 bar pressure. Micro-sprinklers cover 2â4 meters and need only 1 bar. Install sprinklers on risers (short vertical pipes) 30â50 cm high. Use a tee fitting on the main line, then a 15 cm nipple, then the sprinkler. Wrap threads with Teflon tape to stop leaks. 

Space sprinklers so their spray overlaps by 30%. For example, if a sprinkler throws 5 meters, place them 7 meters apart. This gives even coverage. Test by running water and watching coverage. Adjust angles. 

Always install a filter before valves and sprinklers. Sand or screen filters (100â200 mesh) stop particles that clog nozzles. Clean the filter weekly. Also install a pressure regulator if your pump gives more than 3 bar. High pressure makes sprinklers mist and waste water. 

For drip irrigation, you use valves and a filter but no sprinklers. Instead, connect drip tape or drip lines. Each row gets a valve if you want separate control. Turn valves slowly to avoid water hammer that cracks pipes. After installation, flush lines for 5 minutes before closing ends. Check for leaks at every joint. A well-designed valve and sprinkler system saves water and time.

lessons.title: Repairing Cracked Pipes in the Field
lessons.body:
Cracked PVC pipes are common in farms due to sun damage, foot traffic, or water hammer. You can repair them in the field with a few tools: hacksaw, PVC primer and cement, a repair coupling, and sandpaper. First, turn off the water and drain the line. Dig around the crack to expose 30 cm of pipe on both sides. Clean the pipe with a damp cloth. 

For small cracks (less than 5 cm), use a repair coupling. Cut out the cracked section with a hacksaw. Cut a new piece of PVC pipe the same length as the removed section plus 10 cm. Dry-fit the repair coupling and new pipe. Mark the depth of the coupling on the pipe. Remove, then apply primer and cement to both pipe ends and inside the coupling. Slide the coupling onto one pipe, then insert the new pipe into the other end. Twist quarter turn and hold 30 seconds. Wipe excess cement. Let cure 2 hours before water. 

For larger cracks or holes, you can use a PVC patch kit. Clean the area, apply primer, then a patch of PVC sheet with cement. Clamp for 1 hour. This is temporary; replace the section when possible. 

If the pipe is brittle from UV, cut back to good plastic before repairing. Otherwise the crack will spread. For emergency repairs, use a rubber boot clamp (available at hardware stores). Slide it over the crack and tighten. This works for up to 2 bar pressure. 

Always keep a repair kit on the farm: hacksaw, primer, cement, couplings, sandpaper, and rubber clamps. After repair, run water and check for leaks. Bury the repaired section or paint it to prevent future UV damage. Proper repair saves water and money.

lessons.title: Winterizing and Storing Pipes in Off-Season
lessons.body:
In many parts of Africa, off-season means dry months or cold nights. Even if you don't have freezing winters, you should prepare pipes for storage. First, drain all water from pipes. Open all valves and drain plugs. Use a compressor or bicycle pump to blow air through lines if possible. Water left in pipes can grow algae, breed mosquitoes, and crack pipes if it freezes. 

For above-ground pipes, disconnect them from the water source. Remove sprinklers and valves. Clean them with fresh water and dry in shade. Store in a dry, shaded room. Hang pipes vertically or lay flat, not on sharp edges. Avoid stacking heavy items on top. If pipes are buried, you can leave them, but blow out water and cap ends. 

In areas with frost, bury pipes below the frost line (usually 60 cm deep) or use insulation. For small gardens, you can wrap exposed pipes with foam insulation or old blankets. But in most of Africa, frost is rare. The bigger risk is heat and UV. So store pipes indoors or under a tarp. 

Before storing, inspect for cracks or UV damage. Repair any damage. Clean fittings with a wire brush. Apply a thin coat of silicone grease to rubber seals (if any). Store cement and primer in airtight containers away from heat. 

When you restart the system, flush lines for 5 minutes. Check for leaks. Replace any damaged parts. A good off-season routine doubles the life of your PVC pipes. It also saves you money on replacements. Make a checklist: drain, clean, repair, store, and cover.

lessons.title: Project: Building a Drip Irrigation System for a Vegetable Plot
lessons.body:
For a 10m x 10m vegetable plot, you can build a drip irrigation system using PVC pipes and drip tape. You need: 20mm uPVC pipe for main line, 16mm drip tape with emitters every 30cm, a filter, a ball valve, a tee, and end caps. You also need a water source (tap or tank) and a 200-liter drum if using gravity. 

Start by laying out your plot. Make beds 1m wide with 40cm paths. Run a main PVC line along one side of the plot. Connect it to your water source. Install a filter and valve right after the source. Then run 16mm drip tape along each bed. Use a hole punch to make holes in the main line for each drip tape. Insert a small connector (barbed tee) and attach the drip tape. Fold the end of the drip tape and secure with a figure-8 end cap. 

For gravity feed, place a 200-liter drum on a stand 1.5m high. Connect the drum to the main line. Fill the drum and let water flow. You may need to clean the filter daily. For pressure, use a small pump (0.5 HP) with a pressure regulator set to 1 bar. 

Test the system: turn on water and check that every emitter drips. If some don't, check for clogs. Flush the drip tape monthly by opening the end caps. 

This system uses 50% less water than sprinklers. It also reduces weeds because water goes only to plant roots. Cost: about $50â$80 for a 10x10m plot. Maintenance: clean filter weekly, flush tape monthly, repair leaks immediately. With care, drip tape lasts 2â3 seasons; PVC main line lasts 10+ years. This project will give you healthier vegetables and save labor.

quiz.q: What is the best type of PVC pipe for a small farm irrigation main line?
quiz.explanation: uPVC is strong, handles pressure, and resists UV better than other types.

quiz.q: How deep should you bury a PVC main line to protect it from sun and tools?
quiz.explanation: 30â40 cm is deep enough to protect from UV, animals, and most farm tools.

quiz.q: What should you apply to PVC pipe before cementing a joint?
quiz.explanation: Primer cleans and softens the plastic so cement bonds properly.

quiz.q: How long should you hold a cemented PVC joint before releasing?
quiz.explanation: 30 seconds allows the cement to set enough to hold the joint.

quiz.q: What is the minimum recommended pressure for a small farm irrigation pump?
quiz.explanation: 1 bar is enough for most drip and sprinkler systems on small farms.

quiz.q: Why should you install a filter before sprinklers?
options: B) To stop debris clogging nozzles
quiz.explanation: Filters trap particles that would block small sprinkler openings.

quiz.q: What is the main danger of leaving PVC pipes exposed to African sun?
options: B) UV rays make them brittle
quiz.explanation: UV radiation breaks down the plastic, causing cracks and leaks.

quiz.q: Which paint is best for protecting exposed PVC pipes from UV?
options: B) Light-colored acrylic or latex paint
quiz.explanation: Light colors reflect heat and acrylic/latex sticks well to PVC.

quiz.q: How often should you repaint exposed PVC pipes?
quiz.explanation: Paint degrades over time; reapply every 2â3 years for full protection.

quiz.q: What is the cheapest long-term solution for protecting PVC pipes from UV?
quiz.explanation: Burying eliminates UV exposure entirely and costs only labor.

quiz.q: Which valve type is best for quick on/off control in a garden?
quiz.explanation: Ball valves open and close with a quarter turn, making them fast and easy.

quiz.q: How high should you place a riser for a micro-sprinkler?
quiz.explanation: 30â50 cm raises the sprinkler above the crop for even coverage.

quiz.q: What should you wrap on threaded sprinkler connections to stop leaks?
quiz.explanation: Teflon tape seals threads and prevents water leaks.

quiz.q: How much should sprinkler spray overlap for even coverage?
quiz.explanation: 30% overlap ensures no dry spots between sprinklers.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a pressure regulator in a sprinkler system?
options: B) Reduce pressure to safe level
quiz.explanation: It keeps pressure below the maximum for pipes and sprinklers, preventing damage.

quiz.q: What is the first step when repairing a cracked PVC pipe?
options: B) Turn off water and drain line
quiz.explanation: You must stop water flow and drain the line before any repair.

quiz.q: How long should you let a PVC repair cure before turning water back on?
quiz.explanation: 2 hours allows the cement to reach full strength for most repairs.

quiz.q: What is a temporary field repair for a large crack in a PVC pipe?
quiz.explanation: A rubber boot clamp slides over the crack and tightens to stop leaks.

quiz.q: Why should you cut back to good plastic before repairing a UV-damaged pipe?
options: B) To prevent crack from spreading
D) To fit a smaller coupling
quiz.explanation: Brittle plastic will continue to crack; cutting back ensures a strong repair.

quiz.q: What should you keep in a farm PVC repair kit?
options: B) Hacksaw, primer, cement, couplings, sandpaper
quiz.explanation: These tools allow you to cut, clean, and cement a proper repair.

quiz.q: What is the first step in winterizing or storing PVC pipes?
quiz.explanation: Draining prevents algae, mosquitoes, and freeze damage.

quiz.q: How should you store PVC pipes in the off-season?
options: B) In a dry, shaded place
quiz.explanation: Shade and dryness prevent UV damage and warping.

quiz.q: What should you do to rubber seals before storing valves?
quiz.explanation: Silicone grease keeps rubber seals flexible and prevents cracking.

quiz.q: How long should you flush lines when restarting after storage?
quiz.explanation: 5 minutes flushes out debris and stagnant water.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of drip irrigation over sprinklers?
quiz.explanation: Drip delivers water directly to roots, reducing evaporation and waste.

quiz.q: What size drip tape is commonly used for vegetable plots?
quiz.explanation: 16mm drip tape is standard for small vegetable beds.

quiz.q: How high should a gravity-fed water drum be for drip irrigation?
quiz.explanation: 1.5 m gives about 0.15 bar pressure, enough for drip tape.

quiz.q: How often should you flush drip tape?
quiz.explanation: Monthly flushing removes accumulated sediment and prevents clogs.

quiz.q: What is the approximate cost of a drip system for a 10x10m plot?
quiz.explanation: Materials for a small plot are affordable, around $50â$80.

quiz.q: How long does PVC main line last with basic care?
quiz.explanation: uPVC main lines can last over 10 years if protected and maintained.
